title: Chemical Kinetics
description: How fast reactions go, what controls their speed, and the steps they take.

entries.name: Reaction rate
entries.tagline: How quickly reactants are used up and products appear.

sections.text: The rate of a reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit of time. It is measured in moles per litre per second (M/s).
Reactant concentrations fall, hence the minus sign, and product concentrations rise.

points: Rate depends on the coefficients. For 2A → B, the rate of loss of A is twice the rate of formation of B, so rate = −½ Δ[A]/Δt.
The rate is fastest at the start and slows as the reactants are used up. The initial rate is the rate at time zero.
Speed is raised by higher concentration, higher temperature, a larger surface area for solids, and a catalyst.

quiz.q: What are the usual units of reaction rate?

entries.name: Rate laws and reaction order
entries.tagline: An equation that shows how the rate depends on concentrations.

sections.text: k is the rate constant. The exponents m and n are the orders with respect to A and B. The overall order is m + n.

points: The orders must be found by experiment. They are not the coefficients in the balanced equation, except by coincidence.
Zero order: the rate does not depend on that concentration. First order: doubling the concentration doubles the rate. Second order: doubling it quadruples the rate.

sections.text: Run the reaction several times, changing one concentration at a time, and compare the initial rates. If doubling [A] doubles the rate, the reaction is first order in A. If doubling [A] makes the rate four times faster, it is second order.

quiz.q: Doubling the concentration of A makes the rate four times faster. What is the order in A?

entries.name: Integrated rate laws and half-life
entries.tagline: Equations that tell you the concentration at any time.

facts: [A] = [A]₀ − kt. A plot of [A] against t is a straight line. Half-life t½ = [A]₀ ÷ 2k.
ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt. A plot of ln[A] against t is a straight line. t½ = 0.693 ÷ k, which does not depend on the starting concentration.
1/[A] = 1/[A]₀ + kt. A plot of 1/[A] against t is a straight line. t½ = 1 ÷ (k[A]₀).

sections.text: Plot [A], ln[A] and 1/[A] against time. The graph that is a straight line shows the order.
A first-order reaction has k = 0.0231 min⁻¹. Its half-life is 0.693 ÷ 0.0231 = 30.0 min. After 3 half-lives, 1/8 of the reactant is left.

quiz.q: In a first-order reaction, the half-life…
quiz.a: Is constant and depends only on k

entries.name: Collision theory and activation energy
entries.tagline: Molecules must collide, with enough energy and the right orientation, to react.

sections.text: According to collision theory, a reaction happens only when molecules collide with at least a minimum energy, the activation energy Eₐ, and in a suitable orientation.

points: The energy rises to a peak, the transition state or activated complex, and then falls to the products.
The height of the peak above the reactants is Eₐ. The difference between products and reactants is ΔH.
A catalyst lowers Eₐ, so more collisions are successful.
Higher concentration means more collisions per second.
Higher temperature means more molecules have energy of at least Eₐ, and the collisions are more frequent too. The first effect is the larger one.
A larger surface area exposes more of a solid to collisions.

entries.name: The Arrhenius equation
entries.tagline: How the rate constant depends on temperature.

sections.text: A is the frequency factor, which counts how often collisions occur in a suitable orientation. Eₐ is the activation energy, R is the gas constant, and T is the temperature in kelvin.

points: A plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line with slope −Eₐ/R.
With two measurements: ln(k₂/k₁) = (Eₐ/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂).
A rough rule is that the rate doubles for every 10 °C rise near room temperature, for typical activation energies.

quiz.q: In an Arrhenius plot of ln k against 1/T, the slope equals…

entries.name: Reaction mechanisms
entries.tagline: The step-by-step path that turns reactants into products.

sections.text: Most reactions happen in a series of simple steps called elementary steps. The overall equation only shows the start and finish. The mechanism is the full sequence.

points: For an elementary step, the rate law comes straight from the coefficients. A step A + B → products is first order in A and in B. The number of molecules colliding in the step is its molecularity.
The slowest step is the rate-determining step. It controls the overall rate, like the narrowest part of a pipe.
A reaction intermediate is made in one step and used up in a later step, so it does not appear in the overall equation.
A catalyst is used up in one step and regenerated in a later one.
Step 1 (slow): NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO
Step 2 (fast): NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂
NO₃ is the intermediate. The rate follows the slow step, so rate = k[NO₂]².
